questions.q: What does PHP serialization do to an in-memory object?
o: It encrypts the object so only the server can restore it later
It converts the object into a string that can be stored or sent
It compresses the object only to shrink cookie payload size
It validates every property against a schema before storage
questions.x: Serialization snapshots class name and property values as a string. Deserialization rebuilds the object from that string. PHP uses serialize and unserialize for the two directions.
questions.h: Think of a text snapshot of an object's type and fields. What is the reverse operation called?

questions.q: Which PHP function is at the core of this lab's object injection?
o: json_decode, which rebuilds arrays from a JSON cookie string
unserialize, which rebuilds PHP objects from a crafted string
base64_decode, which alone instantiates classes from cookie bytes
eval, which runs the cookie contents as raw PHP source code
questions.x: unserialize rebuilds a PHP object from a string. If that string is attacker-controlled and a class with a dangerous magic method exists, the attacker can instantiate that class.
questions.h: The bug class is insecure deserialization. Which PHP function performs deserialization of objects?

questions.q: What is a PHP magic method in this exploit's context?
o: A method that can run only after an admin privilege check passes
A method PHP invokes automatically at defined object lifecycle points
A method that encrypts its return value before handing it back
A method reachable only through the reflection API in user code
questions.x: Magic methods use double-underscore names such as __construct, __destruct, and __wakeup. PHP calls them at lifecycle moments, not because application code named them in the request.
questions.h: These methods start with two underscores. PHP calls them without an explicit call in the request handler. When in an object's life do they fire?

questions.q: Why is __destruct especially useful in a deserialization exploit?
o: It runs when the object is first created, during unserialize itself
It runs when the object is destroyed, with no extra method call needed
It encrypts leftover properties so they cannot be read after the request
It runs only when the PHP session file is deleted on disk at logout
questions.x: PHP calls __destruct when the object goes out of scope, typically at the end of the request. If that method deletes a file or runs a command, deserializing the class is enough to trigger it.
questions.h: The dest in __destruct names a lifecycle moment. When is an object destroyed, and must the attacker call that method by name?

questions.q: How was the malicious serialized object delivered in this lab?
o: As a URL query parameter on the product search endpoint page
As the session cookie, which already held a serialized User object
As a JSON field in a POST body sent to the account update form
As a custom HTTP header named X-PHP-Serialized-Session-Data
questions.x: Login sets a session cookie that is Base64-wrapped serialized PHP. Replacing that cookie with a crafted CustomTemplate object is the injection vector.
questions.h: The writeup decodes the session cookie after login and finds a serialized User. Where do you put the gadget instead?

questions.q: What did the backup file expose that made the gadget usable?
o: The admin password stored in plain text next to the class
The CustomTemplate class, including properties and __destruct logic
The server's private SSH key included in a commented block
The database connection string used by the template renderer
questions.x: Requesting CustomTemplate.php would execute it. CustomTemplate.php~ returned source, showing lock_file_path and the unlink inside __destruct. That is what the payload is built from.
questions.h: An HTML comment named CustomTemplate.php. Directly fetching the .php file runs it. What backup suffix did the writeup append instead?

questions.q: In PHP serialization, what does O:14 plus the name CustomTemplate mean?
o: An array of 14 items stored inside a CustomTemplate wrapper
An object of class CustomTemplate, whose name is 14 characters long
A 14-byte Base64 blob labeled as a custom template for cookies
An error object whose numeric identifier in PHP is always 14
questions.x: O means object. The number after O is the byte length of the class name, not an id. CustomTemplate is 14 characters, which is why the payload starts that way.
questions.h: PHP type prefixes use a letter then a length then the name. What does uppercase O stand for, and what does 14 count?

questions.q: What is a gadget in PHP deserialization attacks?
o: A Burp extension that prints serialize strings from HTTP history
An existing class whose magic method performs a useful dangerous action
A PHP setting that disables serialization restrictions for cookies
A cookie prefix that forces unserialize to skip class name checks
questions.x: A gadget is a class already in the application that does something dangerous in a magic method. The attacker does not upload new PHP. They instantiate that existing class via unserialize.
questions.h: The attacker injects an object of a class that already exists. What makes that class useful as a gadget?

questions.q: What dangerous action does CustomTemplate's __destruct perform?
o: It runs a shell command stored in the template_file_path property
It deletes a file by calling unlink on the lock_file_path property
It sends an HTTP request to a URL taken from the template path
It appends object contents to a world-writable application log file
questions.x: When the object is destroyed, __destruct calls unlink on lock_file_path if that path exists. Setting the property to /home/carlos/morale.txt deletes the lab target file.
questions.h: The lab asks you to delete morale.txt. Which PHP function removes a file, and which property does __destruct pass to it?

questions.q: Which of the following is true of this lab's PHP object injection?
o: The session cookie stores JSON, so magic methods cannot run at all
The gadget source is CustomTemplate.php served as live executable PHP
None of these statements are true about this PHP object injection lab
__destruct deletes morale.txt when the object is destroyed
questions.x: The last statement is true. PHP calls __destruct when the object is destroyed, and that method unlinks lock_file_path. The cookie is serialized PHP, not JSON, and the leak is CustomTemplate.php~, not the live .php file. None is wrong because that __destruct claim is true.
questions.h: unserialize does not call __construct. Which magic method runs when the request ends and the object is destroyed?
